The new economics of enterprise AI
news.summary: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?” Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes.

Microsoft says that the severity of the problem will differ from server to server, with some not encountering any problems at all. In a different post, Microsoft urged users not to uninstall the problematic update, instead offering a workaround:Open an elevated Command Prompt on an Exchange ServerEnter the following as a command: "reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f"Reboot the serverThat should help alleviate the issue until Microsoft offers a long-term fix for it.

news.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations

Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions.

news.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world

Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal. After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built. That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.” Not everyone is convinced, however.

Since its molecular structure was deduced in the 1950s, DNA has been hailed by many biologists as the secret of life. They’ve read and studied the information stored in the DNA found in the cells of living organisms, known as their genomes, and claimed that this genetic database must be some kind of blueprint, code script, or computer. But if DNA really does harbor some greater secret about how life works, biologists have yet to find it. In fact, the human genome is less a script than a puzzle that gets harder the closer they look. news.title: AI model decodes the language cells use to communicate
news.summary: As an embryo develops from a small cluster of stem cells, those once “blank slate” cells begin to take on more specialized roles like brain, liver, or muscle cells, and organize themselves into three-dimensional structures such as tissues and organs.The fate of each cell — what type of specialized cell it will become — depends on which genes are turned on or off in the cell. These patterns of gene activity shape the cell’s structure and function, enabling it to take on a specific role in the body.But this decision isn’t up to individual cells. They constantly send and receive chemical signals to and from neighboring cells, which help them understand where they are, what stage of development they are in, and what they should become. These messages spread through multi-step sequences called signaling pathways, which translate external signals into specific changes in gene activity in the cell.For researchers, being able to retrace the sequence of instructions a cell has received would offer a powerful way to understand how tissues develop and how these processes go awry in disease. news.title: Ai for utilities requires capability and control
news.summary: Energy and utility companies are increasingly using AI to transform many aspects of their operations. Common use cases include strengthening cyber and infrastructure defenses, making engineering knowledge easier to find, and reducing the time that employees spend assembling information. Realizing this value requires the same discipline that utilities apply to other consequential technologies, including processes to define operating boundaries, validate performance, and ensure accountability. For an organization responsible for critical energy infrastructure, model capability is only one part of the purchasing decision. Where AI runs, what information it can access, and what authority it receives determine which workloads a utility can responsibly put into production. news.title: Agent sprawl
news.summary: The growth of enterprise AI agent platforms has made it much easier for employees to build and deploy agents to support their own work. But as agent creation becomes more decentralized, enterprises face a new management problem: how to keep track of what agents have been built across the organization. Without that visibility, teams can struggle to find and reuse existing agents, while access to enterprise data and systems can become harder to govern. When this proliferation of agents becomes too difficult to manage, it becomes agent sprawl. In this article, Cohere will explain why proliferation isn’t inherently bad, explore how enterprises tend to manage agent sprawl, and consider an alternative approach that allows variant agents to compete.
